GAS-2026-01.question: Why did my gas bill go up in January?

causes.detail: January's bill covered 35 days. December's covered 28.
Heating degree days rose from 10.6 to 12.9 a day. Your gas use follows the cold closely (R² 0.96).
November's bill used an estimated reading that was 310 kWh too low. December's bill caught those units up, which made December look higher.
The unit rate fell from 6.29p to 5.93p per kWh on 1 January.
The standing charge rose from 34.03p to 35.09p a day.
Neither bill has a credit or a one-off charge.
Once the weather is taken out, daily use changed by less than 1%.
Electricity use did not rise to match, so there is no sign of a switch to electric heating.

GAS-2026-01.answer_markdown: Your gas bill went up by {F1}, from {F2} to {F3}. Two things pushed it up. January's bill covered {F4} instead of {F5} [E1], which added {F6}, and January was colder, which added {F7} [E3][E5]. Two things held it down. December's bill included a catch-up from November's estimated reading, so this change is {F8} smaller than it would otherwise be [E6]. The unit rate also fell, saving {F9} [E4]. Once the weather is taken out, your underlying gas use did not change [E5].

next_steps.action: Send your supplier an actual meter reading each month, so your bills aren't based on estimates.
Compare fixed deals. Your unit rate changes with the price cap every three months.
Nothing to fix for the colder weather or the longer bill. Both even out over the year.

evidence.title: The two bills
evidence.sql:
SELECT bill_id, period_start, period_end, days, units_billed, unit,
       energy_gbp, standing_gbp_per_day, adjustments_gbp, read_type, total_gbp
FROM whybill.bills
WHERE utility = 'gas'
  AND bill_id IN ('GAS-2025-12', 'GAS-2026-01')
ORDER BY period_start

evidence.title: Meter readings
evidence.sql:
SELECT read_date, reading, unit, read_type
FROM whybill.reads
WHERE utility = 'gas'
  AND read_date BETWEEN '2025-10-01' AND '2026-02-01'
ORDER BY read_date

evidence.title: Weather in each bill period
evidence.sql:
SELECT b.bill_id, AVG(w.hdd) AS mean_hdd, COUNT(*) AS days
FROM whybill.bills b
JOIN whybill.weather_daily w
  ON w.day BETWEEN b.period_start AND b.period_end
WHERE b.bill_id IN ('GAS-2025-12', 'GAS-2026-01')
GROUP BY b.bill_id

evidence.title: Gas tariff history
evidence.sql:
SELECT valid_from, valid_to, unit_rate_p_inc_vat, standing_p_per_day
FROM whybill.tariffs
WHERE fuel = 'gas'
  AND valid_from <= '2026-02-01'
  AND (valid_to IS NULL OR valid_to >= '2025-12-01')
ORDER BY valid_from

evidence.title: Weather fit: daily gas use against cold days
evidence.sql:
SELECT b.bill_id, b.units_true / b.days AS units_per_day, AVG(w.hdd) AS mean_hdd
FROM whybill.bills b
JOIN whybill.weather_daily w
  ON w.day BETWEEN b.period_start AND b.period_end
WHERE b.utility = 'gas'
  AND b.period_end < '2025-12-01'
GROUP BY b.bill_id, b.units_true, b.days
ORDER BY b.bill_id DESC
LIMIT 12

evidence.title: Estimated reading and catch-up
evidence.sql:
SELECT bill_id, read_type, units_billed, units_true,
       units_billed - units_true AS correction
FROM whybill.bills
WHERE utility = 'gas'
  AND bill_id IN ('GAS-2025-11', 'GAS-2025-12', 'GAS-2026-01')
ORDER BY period_start

evidence.title: Credits and one-off charges
evidence.sql:
SELECT bill_id, adjustments_gbp, adjustment_note
FROM whybill.bills
WHERE bill_id IN ('GAS-2025-12', 'GAS-2026-01')
ORDER BY period_start

evidence.title: Electricity use in the same periods
evidence.sql:
SELECT bill_id, units_true / days AS units_per_day
FROM whybill.bills
WHERE utility = 'electricity'
  AND bill_id IN ('ELEC-2025-12', 'ELEC-2026-01')
ORDER BY period_start

June's bill covered 28 days. May's covered 31.
Both bills use the same unit rate, 25.63p per kWh.
Both bills use the same standing charge, 51.15p a day.
Both bills use actual meter readings.
Once the weather is taken out, daily use changed by less than 1%.
Gas use did not change to suggest a switch between fuels.

ELEC-2026-06.answer_markdown: Your electricity bill went down by {F1}, from {F2} to {F3}. The biggest reason is a goodwill credit of {F4} on June's bill [E7]. Warmer weather cut the electricity used for heating, which saved {F5} [E3][E5]. June's bill was also shorter, {F6} instead of {F7}, which saved {F8} [E1]. Your prices did not change [E4].

next_steps.action: Nothing to do. The credit is already on this bill, so expect July's bill to be higher without it.

no_note.question: Why did my electricity bill change in April?

causes.detail: Once the weather is taken out, you used 2.2 kWh a day more (14%). No household note explains this.
The unit rate fell from 27.69p to 25.63p per kWh on 1 April.
April's bill covered 30 days. March's covered 31.
The standing charge fell from 54.75p to 51.15p a day.
Gas use per day fell 92% over the same period while electricity rose. This usually means heating moved from gas to electric.
April was warmer (heating degree days fell from 8.7 to 6.1), which would lower your use, not raise it.
Both bills use actual meter readings.
Neither bill has a credit or a one-off charge.

no_note.answer_markdown: Your electricity bill fell by {F1}, from {F2} to {F3}, but that hides a big change. You used {F4} more electricity a day than in March, even though April was warmer [E2][E5]. Use beyond what the weather explains added {F5}. Your gas use fell sharply at the same time [E8], which usually means heating has moved from gas to electricity. A lower unit rate saved {F6} [E4] and one fewer day saved {F7} [E1]. None of your household notes explains the change, so add one if something changed at home.

next_steps.action: Add a household note if something changed at home, such as a heat pump, an electric car or someone working from home.

WATER-2026-06.question: Why did my water bill go up in June and July?

causes.detail: Once the weather is taken out, you used 127 litres a day more (32%). No household note explains it.
A hot, dry summer: the average daily high rose from 15.2 °C to 21.4 °C (R² 0.71).
Both bills use the same charge, £4.35 per m³. The April rise was already in the last bill.
Both bills use the same fixed charge, 23p a day.
Both bills cover 61 days.
Both bills use actual meter readings.
Neither bill has a one-off charge.

WATER-2026-06.answer_markdown: Your water bill went up by {F1}, from {F2} to {F3}, because you used {F4} more water [E1][E2]. Hot, dry weather explains {F5} of that [E3][E5]. The other {F6} is not explained by the weather or by any household note. Extra use that appears suddenly and stays high can be a leak, so check your meter [E2].

next_steps.action: Turn off every tap and appliance, then read your water meter twice, 30 minutes apart. If the number moves, you may have a leak: call your water company.
Nothing to fix for the weather. Summer use usually falls back in autumn.
